910.name: Celtic, Roman & Migration Era
910.description: The territory of modern Slovakia was inhabited by Celtic tribes (Cotini, Boii), lay partly within the Roman limes along the Danube (Pannonia), and experienced successive migrations of Germanic, Hunnic, Avar, and Slavic peoples.

sub_clusters.name: Celtic Tribes & Roman Pannonia Frontier
sub_clusters.description: Celtic oppida (Bratislava-Devín), the Boii and Cotini tribes, Roman military presence along the Danube limes (Gerulata, Brigetio), Marcus Aurelius writing Meditations at Carnuntum near the Slovak border, and the inscription at Trenčín (179 CE) — the northernmost Roman inscription in Central Europe.

sub_clusters.name: Avars & Slavic Settlement
sub_clusters.description: Hunnic and Avar domination, Slavic settlement from the 5th–6th centuries, Samo's Empire (623–658) centred partly in Slovak territory, and the Frankish destruction of the Avar Khaganate opening the way for Slavic state formation.

920.name: Great Moravia & Cyrillo-Methodian Mission
920.description: The Principality of Nitra and Great Moravia represent the foundational moments of Slovak national identity. The mission of Saints Cyril and Methodius (863) brought Christianity and the Slavic liturgy, making Great Moravia the cradle of Slavic literary culture.

sub_clusters.name: Principality of Nitra
sub_clusters.description: Prince Pribina's Principality of Nitra — the first known Slovak political entity — with the consecration of the first Christian church on Slovak territory at Nitra (828). Mojmír I's incorporation of Nitra into Great Moravia (833).

sub_clusters.name: Great Moravia & Slavic Literacy
sub_clusters.description: Great Moravia under Rastislav and Svatopluk as a major Central European power. The mission of Cyril and Methodius (863) created the Glagolitic script and Old Church Slavonic liturgy. Magyar invasions destroyed the state by 907.
key_events: Mission of Saints Cyril and Methodius (863)
Fall of Great Moravia to Magyar invasions (c. 907)

920.name: Within the Kingdom of Hungary: Medieval Period
920.description: For nearly a millennium, Slovak territory was part of the Kingdom of Hungary ('Upper Hungary'). German colonisation, mining towns (Banská Štiavnica, Kremnica), and the development of distinct Slovak ethnic identity within the multi-ethnic Hungarian framework.

sub_clusters.name: Early Hungarian Rule & Mongol Invasion
sub_clusters.description: Hungarian incorporation of Slovak lands, the Battle of Pressburg (907), development of the county system, German colonisation of mining towns, the catastrophic Mongol invasion (1241–42) devastating Upper Hungary, and Matthew Csák's powerful domain.

sub_clusters.name: Mining Towns & Late Medieval Flourishing
sub_clusters.description: The golden age of Slovak mining towns: Kremnica mint (producing the famous golden ducats), Banská Štiavnica's silver mines, urban Magdeburg Law privileges, the University of Istropolitana in Bratislava (1465), and Matthias Corvinus's cultural influence.

930.name: Ottoman Wars & Bratislava as Hungarian Capital
930.description: After the Battle of Mohács (1526), Slovakia became the core of Royal Hungary, with Bratislava (Pressburg/Pozsony) serving as the Hungarian capital and coronation city from 1536 to 1783. Anti-Habsburg uprisings and Ottoman frontier warfare defined the era.

sub_clusters.name: Bratislava as Hungarian Capital
sub_clusters.description: After the Ottoman capture of Buda (1541), Bratislava became the capital of Royal Hungary. Eleven Hungarian kings were crowned in St. Martin's Cathedral. The city became a centre of Renaissance and later Counter-Reformation culture.
key_events: Bratislava becomes Hungarian capital and coronation city (1536)

sub_clusters.name: Anti-Habsburg Uprisings
sub_clusters.description: Stephen Bocskai's uprising (1604–06), the Thököly Uprising (1678–85), and Francis II Rákóczi's War of Independence (1703–11) — all significantly fought on Slovak territory — against Habsburg centralisation and Counter-Reformation.

940.name: Slovak National Awakening
940.description: The Slovak National Awakening produced the codification of the Slovak literary language (Ľudovít Štúr, 1843), the 1848 Slovak uprising, the Matica slovenská cultural institution, and persistent struggles against Hungarian Magyarisation policies.

sub_clusters.name: Štúr Generation & Language Codification
sub_clusters.description: Anton Bernolák's first codification (1787), Ján Kollár's pan-Slavic ideas, and Ľudovít Štúr's definitive codification of standard Slovak (1843) based on Central Slovak dialects. The 1848 Slovak National Council and military campaign for autonomy within Hungary.
key_events: Ľudovít Štúr codifies the Slovak literary language (1843)

sub_clusters.name: Magyarisation & Resistance
sub_clusters.description: Post-1867 Compromise: aggressive Magyarisation closed Slovak schools (from 1,900 to 440 by 1914), dissolved Matica slovenská (1875), and suppressed Slovak political activity. Mass emigration to the United States (500,000+ by 1914).

950.name: Czechoslovakia & First Slovak State
950.description: Slovakia joined Czechoslovakia (1918) but tensions over Czech centralism led to the establishment of a Nazi-puppet Slovak State (1939–1945) under Jozef Tiso, which participated in the Holocaust and was challenged by the Slovak National Uprising (1944).

sub_clusters.name: First Czechoslovak Republic
sub_clusters.description: The Pittsburgh Agreement (1918) promised Slovak autonomy within Czechoslovakia. Rapid modernisation under the First Republic but growing tensions over Czech centralisation and the Slovak autonomy movement led by Andrej Hlinka's People's Party.

sub_clusters.name: Nazi Puppet State & Slovak National Uprising
sub_clusters.description: The First Slovak Republic (1939–1945) under Father Jozef Tiso — a Nazi client state that deported 70,000 Jews to death camps. The Slovak National Uprising (August–October 1944) represented armed resistance but was crushed by German forces.

950.name: Communist Czechoslovakia & Normalisation
950.description: Slovakia within communist Czechoslovakia experienced industrialisation (transforming from an agrarian to an industrial society), the 1968 federalisation (the only lasting Prague Spring reform), and 'normalisation' repression.

sub_clusters.name: Stalinism & Slovak Industrialisation
sub_clusters.description: Expulsion of ethnic Hungarians and Germans, Stalinist purges (Vladimír Clementis executed, Gustav Husák imprisoned), massive industrialisation transforming Slovakia from an agricultural to an industrial economy, and the Slovak quest for autonomy.

sub_clusters.name: 1968 Federation & Normalisation Era
sub_clusters.description: The constitutional law of federation (October 1968) — the only Prague Spring reform that survived — created the Slovak Socialist Republic. Gustav Husák's 'normalisation' from Bratislava Castle, the candle demonstration (March 1988), and growing dissent.

960.name: Slovak Independence & EU Integration
960.description: The Velvet Revolution (1989), the Velvet Divorce creating independent Slovakia (January 1, 1993), Vladimír Mečiar's authoritarian tendencies, the reform era leading to EU and NATO accession (2004), and euro adoption (2009).

sub_clusters.name: Velvet Divorce & Mečiar Era
sub_clusters.description: The Velvet Revolution's Slovak dimension (Public Against Violence movement), negotiations with Czech leaders, the Velvet Divorce (January 1, 1993) creating an independent Slovak Republic, and Vladimír Mečiar's controversial authoritarian-leaning governments.

sub_clusters.name: EU/NATO Accession & Euro Adoption
sub_clusters.description: Mikuláš Dzurinda's reform governments, NATO and EU accession (2004), euro adoption (January 1, 2009) — making Slovakia the only Visegrád country in the eurozone — the Kia/VW automotive boom, Robert Fico's return, the Ján Kuciak journalist murder (2018), and contemporary political developments.
